name: Otto von Bismarck
info: Otto von Bismarck (1815–1898), a Prussian Junker who became minister president of Prussia in 1862, unified Germany through three wars and governed the German Empire as its first chancellor from 1871 until Wilhelm II dismissed him in 1890.

facts.born: 1 April 1815 at Schönhausen, a family estate west of Berlin in Prussian Saxony; son of Ferdinand von Bismarck, a Junker landowner and former officer, and Wilhelmine Mencken, daughter of a senior Berlin official
facts.died: 30 July 1898, just after midnight, at Friedrichsruh near Hamburg, aged 83, after years of failing health and gangrene in his foot
facts.role: Member of the Prussian United Landtag (1847) and Landtag (1849); envoy to the Federal Diet at Frankfurt (1851–1859); ambassador to Russia and to France (1862); Minister President and Foreign Minister of Prussia (1862–1890); first Chancellor of the German Empire (1871–1890); Count (1865), Prince (1871), Duke of Lauenburg (1890)
facts.known: the 'iron and blood' speech of 1862; the wars against Denmark, Austria and France and the unification of Germany in 1871; the Kulturkampf against the Catholic Church; the Anti-Socialist Laws; sickness, accident and old-age insurance; the alliance system that kept the great powers at peace; the Congress of Berlin and the Berlin Conference; Germanisation policies against the Poles

t: Appointed minister president of Prussia in 1862 to break a deadlock over the army budget, Bismarck governed for years without a legal budget and used three short wars, against Denmark, Austria and France, to unite Germany under Prussia by 1871.

As imperial chancellor he kept the new empire at peace through a web of alliances, while at home he fought the Catholic Church, banned socialist organisations, pressed Germanisation on the Poles and other minorities and created the first welfare state to win workers from socialism.

Dismissed by Wilhelm II in 1890, he spent his last years attacking the emperor in his memoirs; historians praise his diplomacy but argue that his authoritarian system, with no check on the emperor, left Germany a dangerous inheritance.
dyk: The only known recording of Bismarck's voice was made on an Edison phonograph in 1889; in it he quoted, among other things, the first verse of 'La Marseillaise', which a biographer took as a jibe at the French nineteen years after the war.
ev: Born at Schönhausen, a noble family estate west of Berlin
Appointed Minister President and Foreign Minister of Prussia in September and gives his 'iron and blood' speech to the Budget Committee
Prussia and Austria defeat Denmark in the Second Schleswig War, and Denmark gives up the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein
Prussia defeats Austria at Königgrätz in a seven-week war, and the German Confederation gives way to the North German Confederation
Wilhelm I is proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles after the defeat of France, and Bismarck becomes the first Imperial Chancellor
Abandons the Kulturkampf and, after two attempts on the emperor's life, has the Reichstag pass the Anti-Socialist Laws
Resigns at Wilhelm II's insistence on 18 March and is succeeded by Leo von Caprivi
Dies at Friedrichsruh, where he is entombed in the Bismarck Mausoleum

sections.early:
Otto von Bismarck was born on 1 April 1815 at Schönhausen, a noble family estate west of Berlin in Prussian Saxony. His father, Ferdinand von Bismarck, was a Junker landowner and former Prussian officer of modest means; his mother, Wilhelmine Mencken, was the well-educated daughter of a senior government official in Berlin, from a family of civil servants and academics. In 1816 the family moved to its Pomeranian estate, Kniephof, northeast of Stettin, where he spent his childhood. Others saw him as a typical backwoods Junker, an image he encouraged by wearing uniform, but he was well educated and cosmopolitan, with a gift for conversation and a knowledge of English, French, Italian, Polish and Russian.

After school he studied law at Göttingen, where he befriended the American John Lothrop Motley, and at Berlin from 1833 to 1835. He began training as a lawyer in Aachen and Potsdam but soon resigned, having put his career at risk by taking unauthorised leave to pursue two English girls. After a shortened military service he ran the family estates at Schönhausen. Around the age of thirty he formed an intense friendship with Marie von Thadden-Trieglaff; a month after her death he asked for the hand of her cousin, Johanna von Puttkamer, a deeply religious woman, whom he married on 28 July 1847. They had three children, Marie, Herbert and Wilhelm.
sections.rise:
In 1847 Bismarck entered the new Prussian United Landtag, chosen through the ultra-conservative Gerlach brothers, and won a name as a royalist reactionary with a gift for stinging rhetoric who defended the king's divine right. In the revolution of 1848 he tried to raise the peasants of his estate to march on Berlin for the king. Elected to the Landtag in 1849, he then opposed German unification, fearing Prussia would lose its independence. From 1851 to 1859 he was Prussia's envoy to the Federal Diet in Frankfurt, where he insisted on equal treatment with the Austrian envoy, fought a duel that ended without injury, and grew less reactionary and more pragmatic, convinced that Prussia must ally with other German states against Austria. He then served as ambassador to Russia and, in 1862, to France.

In 1862 the liberal majority of the Prussian Landtag refused to fund King Wilhelm I's reorganisation of the army, and the king, advised by Albrecht von Roon, appointed Bismarck Minister President and Foreign Minister on 23 September. Arguing that the constitution had a "legal loophole" where no budget was passed, he kept collecting taxes on the 1861 budget for four years, restricted the press and remained deeply unpopular; in 1863 a liberal coalition won over two-thirds of the seats. On 30 September 1862 he told the Budget Committee that the great questions of the time would be decided not by speeches and majority decisions "but by iron and blood".
sections.deeds:
With Roon's reorganised army and Moltke's strategy, Bismarck used three short wars to unify Germany without Austria. In 1864 Prussia and Austria defeated Denmark over Schleswig and Holstein. In 1866 he provoked war with Austria over the duchies, allied secretly with Italy and, after the victory at Königgrätz, insisted on a soft peace with no annexations from Austria; the German Confederation was replaced by the Prussian-led North German Confederation. In 1870 he published an edited version of the Ems Dispatch to provoke France into war. The South German states rallied to Prussia, the French armies were captured at Sedan and Metz, and on 18 January 1871 Wilhelm I was proclaimed German Emperor at Versailles. France ceded Alsace and part of Lorraine.

As the empire's first chancellor and Prussia's minister president, Bismarck controlled both foreign and domestic policy. Abroad, wanting no more territory, he isolated France and bound the other powers in alliances: the League of the Three Emperors, the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879, the Triple Alliance in 1882 and the secret Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1887. He helped negotiate the settlement of the Congress of Berlin after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 and organised the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885, as Germany acquired colonies from Togoland to German New Guinea. At home he gave Germany sickness insurance in 1883, accident insurance in 1884 and old-age and disability insurance in 1889, to tie workers to the state and draw them from the Social Democrats.
sections.opponents:
Bismarck's domestic rule was repressive. From 1871 his Kulturkampf against the Catholic Church imprisoned or exiled all Prussian bishops and many priests, expelled the Jesuits, banned most religious orders and cut off state payments to the clergy; the Catholics answered by building the Centre Party, and he abandoned the campaign in 1878. That year, blaming two attempts on the emperor's life on the socialists without evidence, he passed the Anti-Socialist Laws, under which some 330 workers' organisations were banned, around 1,500 people imprisoned and nearly 900 expelled from their towns. His government pressed Germanisation on the Danes, the people of Alsace-Lorraine and above all the Poles: Polish was pushed out of schools and administration, more than 30,000 people without German citizenship were expelled from the eastern provinces in 1885–1886, and a Settlement Commission bought estates for German farmers. In 1861 he had written privately of the Poles that "we have no choice but to wipe them out".

Critics then and since have judged him harshly. Queen Victoria called him "overbearing, violent, grasping, and unprincipled". Jonathan Steinberg describes a violent temper, intolerance of opposition and paranoia that made the Kulturkampf relentless, and quotes the British ambassador Odo Russell: "The demonic is stronger in him than in any man I know." Evans calls him "intimidating and unscrupulous". His giving in to the demand for Alsace-Lorraine, which turned France into a permanent enemy, is often called his main mistake.
sections.last:
Wilhelm I died in 1888 and his son Frederick III after only 99 days, leaving the throne to the young Wilhelm II, who wanted to govern himself and to pursue rapid expansion. The two soon quarrelled. Bismarck tried to make the Anti-Socialist Laws permanent and, in an outburst, admitted he wanted the socialists to agitate until a violent clash gave a pretext to crush them; Wilhelm replied that he would not open his reign with a bloody campaign against his own subjects. Bismarck refused to sign a proclamation on the protection of workers and, when his coalition lost its majority, invited the Centre Party leader Ludwig Windthorst to talks without informing the emperor. After a furious argument he resigned at Wilhelm's insistence on 18 March 1890, aged 75, and was succeeded by Leo von Caprivi.

He was given the honorary rank of colonel-general with the dignity of field marshal and the title of Duke of Lauenburg, without the duchy, which he regarded as a mockery of his ambition. Elected to the Reichstag, he never took his seat, humiliated at being forced to a second ballot by a Social Democrat. In resentful retirement at Friedrichsruh he wrote his memoirs, Thoughts and Memories, attacking Wilhelm II and presenting himself favourably, and published the secret Reinsurance Treaty. After his wife's death in 1894 his health worsened; he refused treatment for gangrene in his foot, and died just after midnight on 30 July 1898. His sarcophagus calls him "A loyal German servant of Emperor Wilhelm I".
sections.legacy:
Bismarck's lasting legacy is the unification of Germany, which became one of the most powerful nations in Europe. Jonathan Steinberg calls his achievements of 1862–1871 "the greatest diplomatic and political achievement by any leader in the last two centuries". Diplomatic historians praise his peace after 1871: A. J. P. Taylor called him "an honest broker of peace", Eric Hobsbawm the "undisputed world champion at the game of multilateral diplomatic chess", and William L. Langer credits him with steering Europe through a dangerous period without serious conflict between the great powers. His welfare laws drew praise from Theodore Roosevelt in 1916. His system did not survive him: the Reinsurance Treaty lapsed after 1890, and Wilhelm II's Weltpolitik united the other powers against Germany before the First World War.

Others see a darker inheritance. Steinberg, Evans, Taylor and Palmer regard him as an ambivalent figure who left no system for less skilled successors, and by allowing no effective constitutional check on the emperor he placed a time bomb in the foundation of the state he created. Henry Kissinger argues that he so undermined liberalism that the Weimar Republic could never make it succeed. In imperial Germany nationalists built monuments and Bismarck towers to him, while Catholics, Social Democrats and Poles remembered him with hostility. Robert Gerwarth shows how the Bismarck myth, built up after his death, became a weapon against the Weimar Republic.

summary: Otto von Bismarck, a Prussian Junker and minister president from 1862, unified Germany through wars against Denmark, Austria and France and served as the German Empire's first chancellor until 1890. He kept Europe's great powers at peace and created the first welfare state, while fighting the Catholic Church, the socialists and the Poles, and leaving an authoritarian state that historians still debate.

Friedrich Darmstaedter, Bismarck and the Creation of the Second Reich (Russel & Russel, 2008)
